title: Backpressure
subtitle: Pull-based flow control, dynamic pause/resume, and bounded producer memory buffers.
keyTakeaways: Kafka's pull-based consumer architecture naturally provides backpressure: consumers only fetch as much data as they have capacity to process.
When downstream dependencies slow down, consumers can dynamically pause partition fetching (`consumer.pause()`) while continuing background heartbeats to prevent rebalances.
Producers enforce backpressure using bounded memory buffers (`buffer.memory`): when full, producers block or throw `TimeoutException` rather than crashing with out-of-memory errors.
architectureDiagram:
PULL-BASED FLOW CONTROL & CONSUMER PAUSE/RESUME
[ Broker Partition Log ]
         |
         v (Pull: Consumer requests batch of 50 records)
[ Consumer Worker Pool ] ---> Slow Database (Database connection pool exhausted!)
         |
   Buffer Filling Up!
         v
[ consumer.pause([Partition 0]) ]
- Consumer stops fetching new messages from Partition 0
- Background heartbeat thread CONTINUES running (No rebalance triggered!)
- Database recovers -> [ consumer.resume([Partition 0]) ] -> Normal fetching resumes

sections.heading: Pull-Based Consumption vs Push Overload
sections.body: In push-based messaging architectures (like standard HTTP webhooks or naive RabbitMQ configurations), brokers push messages to consumers as soon as they arrive. If traffic surges 10x, the broker floods workers faster than they can write to backing databases, exhausting memory and causing OOM crashes. Kafka solves this by using a Pull-Based model: consumers issue fetch requests only when ready for more work.
bullets: Consumer Flow Control: Consumers regulate batch size via `max.poll.records` (default: 500) and byte limits (`max.partition.fetch.bytes`).

Dynamic Pause and Resume: If a downstream database begins returning connection pool errors, the consumer calls `consumer.pause([partition])`. The client stops requesting data for that partition while maintaining heartbeat pings (`consumer.poll(0)`), preventing coordinator timeouts until `consumer.resume()` is called.

sections.heading: Producer Backpressure and Broker Quotas
sections.body: Backpressure must also operate on the producer side when network bandwidth or broker write limits saturate.
bullets: Producer Buffer Limits (`buffer.memory`): Producers buffer unsent messages in memory (default: 32 MB). If the broker network is saturated and buffers fill, `producer.send()` blocks up to `max.block.ms` (default: 60s) before throwing an exception, forcing the upstream application to throttle.

Broker Client Quotas: Kafka brokers can enforce network bandwidth and request rate quotas per user or client ID, returning produce throttling metrics to prevent noisy neighbors from exhausting broker I/O.

tradeOffs.pros: Natural backpressure; workers never consume more than their processing capacity; zero OOM crashes under traffic spikes.
tradeOffs.cons: Consumers must actively poll; can introduce a few milliseconds of latency when waiting on empty topic polls.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput data ingestion, batch database writers, and resilient microservice architectures.

tradeOffs.pros: Lowest possible latency for single events; broker immediately pushes data upon arrival.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires complex reactive backpressure protocols (RSocket, reactive-streams) to prevent consumer memory starvation.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time user UI updates and streaming audio/video chat.

interviewTip: Highlight the advantage of pull over push in system design: 'Because Kafka uses a pull-based model, consumers inherently control their own consumption rate. If downstream databases slow down, consumers naturally throttle without being overwhelmed by push floods, and can use `consumer.pause()` to temporarily halt fetching while maintaining heartbeats.'
